notes:
Task and constraints: Return the index of the first character occurring once in s, or -1 if every character repeats; the original string order determines which unique character is first.
Idea: Counter(s) counts each character. enumerate then scans left to right and returns the first index whose character count equals one; if none qualifies, it returns -1.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting separates the question of uniqueness from position, letting a second pass preserve the earliest occurrence.
Invariant: Before each index i is checked, all earlier positions have been examined and none contained a character with total frequency one.
Edge cases: Empty input returns -1; "leetcode" returns index zero; a string where all characters repeat returns -1. Python Counter handles arbitrary characters, not only lowercase letters.
Complexity: Counting and scanning are O(n) time; Counter stores O(u) distinct characters.
complexity_reason: The string is counted and scanned once, and Counter stores one entry for each distinct character.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the earliest index of a character appearing exactly once, returning -1 if no such character exists; this implementation assumes lowercase a-z.
Idea: The first loop counts characters in a 26-element array. The second loop checks positions in order and returns the first whose count is one, otherwise returning -1.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed frequency table records total occurrences so the second scan can identify the first unique character without repeated searches.
Invariant: Before checking index i, all preceding indices have failed the unique-count condition, so any returned index is the earliest valid one.
Edge cases: Empty string returns -1; "leetcode" returns 0; if every character repeats, the method returns -1. Index c-'a' assumes lowercase English letters, and charAt uses valid indices from zero to length-1.
Complexity: Two string scans take O(n) time; the 26-entry array gives O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Both passes scan the string once and the count array always has 26 integer entries.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum absolute path length to a file in a newline/tab-indented filesystem description; directory separators count as one character each.
Idea: Each line's tab count gives its depth and name removes that indentation. For files, a dot in the name triggers best=max(best,lengths[depth]+len(name)); for directories, lengths[depth+1] stores parent path length plus directory name and slash.
Technique and why it applies: Depth-indexed path lengths compute parent prefixes without constructing every full path, using indentation to identify the parent.
Invariant: lengths[d] is the absolute path length of the parent directory at depth d, including the trailing separator expected before its child.
Edge cases: An empty input yields zero; a file at depth zero uses just its name length; nested directories accumulate one separator each. This code treats any dot in a name as indicating a file.
Complexity: Splitting and scanning characters takes O(n) time; lines and lengths arrays use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The input is split into lines and each line is processed once; the lines and depth-length array require linear storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the longest absolute path to a file from a tab-indented description, counting directory separators but not indentation tabs.
Idea: split creates lines and lengths stores path lengths by depth. Each line's leading tabs determine d; a name containing a dot updates best, while a directory sets lengths[d+1] to lengths[d]+name.length()+1.
Technique and why it applies: Depth-indexed dynamic state reuses the parent path length and avoids building full strings for every directory path.
Invariant: lengths[d] records the prefix length for a directory at depth d, including the separator needed before its children.
Edge cases: An empty description returns zero; a top-level file has path length equal to its name; nested directories add one slash per level. split("\\n",-1) retains trailing empty lines, and the code identifies files by a dot in the name.
Complexity: The lines and their characters are scanned once for O(n) time; the line array and lengths array use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Splitting and scanning all lines takes linear time, and both the line array and depth-indexed lengths array scale with input size.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given t formed by shuffling s and adding one character, return the added character without counting every possible character.
Idea: x starts at zero and XORs ord(c) for every character in the concatenation s+t. The matching characters cancel in pairs, leaving the code point of the extra character, which chr converts back to a one-character string.
Technique and why it applies: XOR is self-inverse, so equal code points cancel regardless of their order in the two strings.
Invariant: After processing any prefix of s+t, x is the XOR of all code points processed; after both strings, all shared character occurrences cancel.
Edge cases: If s is empty, the only character in t remains; repeated letters cancel by occurrence count; Unicode characters work because ord and chr operate on code points.
Complexity: The combined strings are scanned once for O(n) time, with one integer accumulator giving O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Every character in s and t is XORed once, and only the accumulator x is retained.

notes:
Task and constraints: Recover the one extra character in t, which contains the characters of s plus one additional occurrence; the order may differ.
Idea: The int variable x starts at zero. The first loop XORs each char from s.toCharArray() into x, and the second does the same for t.toCharArray(); return (char)x converts the unmatched value to a Java char.
Technique and why it applies: XOR cancellation ignores order and duplicate arrangement, leaving the one value whose multiplicity differs by one.
Invariant: x is the XOR of every character processed so far; after both loops, paired equal characters contribute zero and the remaining XOR is the added character.
Edge cases: Empty s leaves the sole character of t; repeated characters cancel according to their occurrences across both strings; Java char processes UTF-16 code units, which suits typical lowercase constraints but differs from full Unicode code points for supplementary symbols.
Complexity: Both char-array loops visit every character once, giving O(n) time; x is the only extra state, so auxiliary space is O(1) apart from temporary arrays.
complexity_reason: The two loops visit each character once and maintain only one integer XOR accumulator.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the final number after repeatedly eliminating every other number from 1..n, alternating scan direction; simulating the list would use unnecessary space.
Idea: head tracks the first surviving value, step the gap between survivors, remaining the survivor count, and left the direction. Each round advances head when scanning leftward or when an odd count forces the first item to be removed, then halves remaining and doubles step.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative state compression tracks the arithmetic progression of survivors instead of storing the entire list.
Invariant: Survivors form an arithmetic progression beginning at head with difference step and count remaining.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1 without a round; n=2 advances head to 2; odd remaining counts advance head even during a right-to-left pass because the first survivor is removed. step doubles each round.
Complexity: remaining is halved each iteration, so time is O(log n) and space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each iteration halves remaining and updates three scalar state values, giving logarithmic time and constant space.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the last survivor in alternating left-to-right and right-to-left elimination of 1..n, tracking the survivor sequence rather than allocating a list.
Idea: head is the first survivor, step is the gap, remaining is the count, and left records direction. Each pass conditionally advances head, halves remaining, doubles step, and flips left.
Technique and why it applies: The survivors always form an arithmetic progression, so four scalar variables summarize the entire current round.
Invariant: The current surviving sequence starts at head, has spacing step, and contains remaining values; the update transforms this sequence to the next round's survivors.
Edge cases: n=1 returns 1; n=2 returns 2 after one leftward pass; an odd remaining count advances head on a rightward pass. The input is positive, and step doubling remains within expected constraints.
Complexity: The count is halved each round, yielding O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The loop repeatedly halves remaining and updates a fixed number of int and boolean variables.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether s can be obtained by deleting characters from t while preserving order; characters may be skipped but never reordered.
Idea: i points to the next character required from s. The loop scans t, advances i when t's current character matches s[i], and returns whether i reached len(s).
Technique and why it applies: A greedy two-pointer scan matches each required character at its earliest available position, leaving the largest possible suffix of t for later matches.
Invariant: After each scanned character, s[:i] has been matched as a subsequence of the portion of t already processed.
Edge cases: Empty s returns true; if t is empty and s is nonempty, the result is false; repeated characters are matched one occurrence at a time. The i<len(s) guard prevents indexing past s.
Complexity: Scanning t and accounting for s takes O(n+m) time and O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: The method scans t once and stores only the index i; it does not create a separate subsequence.

notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether s is a subsequence of t, meaning all characters of s appear in t in the same order; unmatched characters in t may be skipped.
Idea: i tracks the next required character in s. The for loop advances j across t and increments i when s.charAt(i) matches t.charAt(j); success means i equals s.length().
Technique and why it applies: Greedy two pointers choose the earliest possible match for each character, preserving the maximum remaining suffix for future matches.
Invariant: The first i characters of s have been matched in order within t[0..j), and no later match can undo that prefix.
Edge cases: Empty s returns true; nonempty s with empty t returns false; i<s.length() guards charAt(i) against out-of-range access. Java char comparisons use UTF-16 code units.
Complexity: Each character of t is inspected once for O(n+m) time; only two indices are maintained, giving O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The loop scans t once and maintains only indices i and j.

notes:
Task and constraints: Validate that each integer is a legal byte and that each UTF-8 sequence has a valid leading byte followed by the required continuation bytes.
Idea: At index i, the code bounds-checks x and identifies sequence length from its leading bits. It rejects incomplete sequences, verifies each continuation value is in 0..255 with top bits 10, then advances i by the sequence length.
Technique and why it applies: Bit masks classify UTF-8 leading and continuation patterns without converting the bytes to text.
Invariant: At the start of each outer iteration, all prior bytes have been consumed as complete valid sequences, and i points to the next sequence's lead byte.
Edge cases: ASCII bytes use count one; a leading byte without enough following bytes fails; continuation bytes cannot start a sequence. The code checks byte ranges but does not enforce Unicode scalar restrictions such as overlong forms or surrogate encodings beyond these leading-bit rules.
Complexity: Every byte is examined a bounded number of times for O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The outer pointer advances across each byte sequence and the inner loop checks its continuation bytes; only counters are stored.

notes:
Task and constraints: Verify integer values encode UTF-8 byte sequences using valid lead-byte patterns and continuation bytes; values outside the byte range are rejected.
Idea: The loop checks data[i] in 0..255, determines count from the high bits, rejects unsupported leads or truncated sequences, validates following bytes with a 10 prefix, then advances i by count.
Technique and why it applies: Bit masks distinguish one- through four-byte sequence prefixes and ensure each following byte has the required continuation pattern.
Invariant: Every byte before i belongs to a complete sequence that passed these checks; i always points to the next unprocessed leading byte.
Edge cases: ASCII bytes pass as single-byte sequences; a four-byte prefix with fewer than four available bytes fails; a continuation byte used as a lead is rejected. This checks byte-pattern validity, not every Unicode scalar restriction such as overlong encodings.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) because each byte is checked a bounded number of times; only a few integer variables are used, so space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each input byte is validated once as a lead or continuation, with a fixed number of counters and indices.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decode nested expressions such as 3[a2[c]] by repeating bracketed content the specified number of times; runtime necessarily depends on decoded output size.
Idea: Digit characters accumulate num. At [, counts and the current prefix are pushed and current state resets. At ], the previous prefix is popped and joined with curr repeated counts.pop() times; ordinary characters append to curr.
Technique and why it applies: Two stacks preserve the repeat count and prefix for each nesting level, allowing inner strings to be decoded before their enclosing repetition.
Invariant: curr is the decoded content for the currently open bracket level, while each stack entry stores the count and prefix needed to resume its parent level.
Edge cases: Plain letters pass through unchanged; multi-digit counts accumulate correctly; nested brackets restore the previous prefix on closing. The input is assumed well-formed, so pops have matching pushes.
Complexity: Processing and constructing output take O(L) time relative to decoded output length L; stacks and intermediate strings use O(L) space.
complexity_reason: Each input character is processed once, while repeated concatenation and the final decoded string require space proportional to output length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decode nested repetition expressions where k[content] repeats content k times; the output may be much larger than the encoded input.
Idea: Digits build num. On [, counts and the prior StringBuilder are pushed and cur resets. On ], the prior builder is restored and cur is appended k times; letters append directly to cur.
Technique and why it applies: Paired stacks preserve each nesting level's multiplier and prefix, so inner content can be completed before repeated insertion into its parent.
Invariant: cur contains decoded content for the current level, and each stack entry holds the multiplier and prefix to resume after the matching closing bracket.
Edge cases: Ordinary letters remain unchanged; multi-digit counts are accumulated in num; nested expressions unwind in last-in-first-out order. The code assumes balanced, well-formed input; StringBuilder avoids immutable-string concatenation on every character.
Complexity: Work is proportional to decoded output length L, and builders/stacks can hold O(L) intermediate content.
complexity_reason: Every encoded character is processed once and repeated content is appended into StringBuilders whose total storage follows decoded output size.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest substring where each character present occurs at least k times; the method recursively splits at any character whose total count is too small.
Idea: If len(s)<k it returns zero. Otherwise Counter counts s; on finding a character with count below k, the method splits s on that character and returns the maximum recursive result among pieces. If none is under-frequency, all of s qualifies.
Technique and why it applies: Divide and conquer uses an under-frequency character as a separator, since no valid substring can include that character while satisfying the frequency rule.
Invariant: Every recursive piece excludes the chosen separator, and any valid substring lies entirely within one resulting piece.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than k return zero; k=1 returns the full string length for nonempty input; a rare character at the edge may produce an empty piece. Repeated splitting can cause quadratic work and deep recursion.
Complexity: The worst-case time is O(n²) due to repeated counting/splitting; recursion and substring storage can use O(n) space along a call path.
complexity_reason: Each recursive call counts and splits its substring, and the worst-case repeated scans are quadratic with recursion and substring storage proportional to input length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest substring in which each present character appears at least k times; characters with global frequency below k act as separators.
Idea: The method returns zero when s.length()<k, counts lowercase letters, and scans s for a character whose count is below k. At the first such character it recursively solves the left and right substrings around a run of under-frequency characters, then takes the maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Divide and conquer removes characters that cannot belong to any valid substring, reducing the problem to independent segments.
Invariant: Any valid answer must lie wholly on one side of a chosen under-frequency character, so the maximum of the recursive segments is sufficient.
Edge cases: A short string returns zero; if all counts meet k, the full length is returned; consecutive rare characters are skipped together before recursing. Index c-'a' assumes lowercase input, and substring creates new strings.
Complexity: Worst-case repeated counting and substring scans take O(n²) time; recursion and allocated substrings use O(n) space under the supplied label.
complexity_reason: The code may recount overlapping substrings across recursive calls, giving O(n²) worst-case time and linear-scale recursion/string storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize the weighted sum F(k) across all cyclic rotations of nums; recomputing each rotation from scratch is unnecessary.
Idea: Empty input returns zero. total is the sum of values, f is the weighted sum for the original order, and best starts at f. For each rotation k, f updates by adding total and subtracting n times the value moved from the end to the front.
Technique and why it applies: A rolling recurrence derives the next rotation's score from the previous score and the array sum, so each rotation update is constant work.
Invariant: At iteration k, f equals the rotation function for the kth rotation and best is the maximum score among rotations processed so far.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return zero; one element returns zero; negative values are handled by the same recurrence. Python integers avoid fixed-width overflow.
Complexity: The initial sum and weighted sum take O(n), followed by O(n) constant-time updates; auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The code computes two initial aggregates and then updates the score once per rotation, storing only scalar totals.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum rotation function F(k)=sum(i*A_k[i]) over all cyclic rotations; the recurrence avoids O(n²) recomputation.
Idea: Empty arrays return zero. The first loop computes total and the original weighted sum f using long. Each next rotation updates f by total minus n times the element moved from the end, and best tracks the maximum before the final cast to int.
Technique and why it applies: The rolling recurrence expresses the next weighted sum from the previous sum and the total of all elements.
Invariant: f is the current rotation's weighted sum, while best stores the largest long score seen so far.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; a single element yields zero; long intermediates reduce overflow risk during multiplication and accumulation, but the final int cast assumes the expected result fits int.
Complexity: Two linear scans give O(n) time and only a few long variables are stored, so extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The method calculates total and initial score in one pass, then updates the score for each remaining rotation using constant state.

notes:
Task and constraints: Minimize operations to reduce positive n to one, halving even values and adjusting odd values by one; the method uses the low bits to choose the adjustment.
Idea: steps increments each iteration. Even n is halved; odd n is decremented when n==3 or n%4==1, otherwise incremented. The loop ends at one.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy bit reasoning chooses the odd adjustment that creates more trailing zero bits for subsequent halving, with three handled as a special case where decrementing is better.
Invariant: n remains a positive integer moving toward one, and steps counts exactly the operations already applied.
Edge cases: n=1 returns zero; n=3 takes two operations by decrementing to two then halving; an odd value congruent to 3 modulo 4 is incremented except for the special case 3. Python integers avoid overflow on n+1.
Complexity: Each operation reduces the magnitude substantially over a bounded number of steps per bit, giving O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The loop updates n and steps only, and each operation reduces the number of significant bits after at most a constant number of adjustments.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum operations to reduce positive int n to one using halving for even values and plus/minus one for odd values.
Idea: x is a long copy of n so incrementing Integer.MAX_VALUE cannot overflow. Even x shifts right; odd x decrements when x==3 or its low two bits are 01, otherwise increments; steps counts operations.
Technique and why it applies: The greedy rule prefers an odd adjustment that creates trailing zero bits and enables more halving, except that 3 should become 2 rather than 4.
Invariant: x remains positive and steps is the number of legal operations performed so far; each iteration moves x toward one.
Edge cases: n=1 returns zero; n=3 follows decrement then halve; using long avoids overflow when an odd int is incremented at the upper bound. Input must be positive.
Complexity: The number of operations is O(log n) and only x and steps are stored, so auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop processes a logarithmic number of bit-reduction steps and maintains only a long value and an int counter.
